ad_body:
My puppy peed six inches from the pee pad. Every single time.

Not on it. Right next to it.

My name is Maureen. I'm 63, I drove a school bus in Reno, Nevada for 22 years, and last spring I adopted Pepper, a 9-month-old shepherd mix, from a rescue.

She's sweet, she's smart, and for two months she peed on my hallway carpet.

I did everything the internet told me.

I bought the big 100-pack of disposable pads from the pet store. I put them by the back door, in the hallway and next to her crate.

She would walk up to the pad, sniff it, turn around, and squat on the carpet right beside it.

I bought treats. I bought a spray that's supposed to make dogs want to go on the pad. I clapped and said "good girl" the one time she put a paw on it.

Nothing changed.

I was scrubbing the carpet with a towel and a bucket every morning. My knees hurt. The hallway smelled no matter how much I cleaned.

My daughter said, "Mom, some dogs just never get it."

I started to think Pepper was one of them.

Then one night I was reading on my phone and found a story written by a woman named Sarah Mitchell.

She ran a county animal shelter in California for 14 years.

She wrote that she watched dog after dog get brought back to her shelter because they kept peeing in the house. One of them was an 8-month-old golden retriever named Charlie. His family brought him back three times for peeing on the carpet.

That part made me put my phone down for a minute.

Then she wrote about something she noticed at the shelter.

Some dogs walked in and used the training pads right away. Other dogs ignored them completely.

The difference was the pad.

When a dog got a pad that other dogs had already used, it went on it almost right away. When it got a brand new pad, it walked right past.

Dogs choose where to pee by smell. A dog's nose has about 300 million scent receptors. Ours has about 6 million.

A brand new disposable pad smells like plastic. To a dog, it doesn't smell like a bathroom spot at all.

That was exactly what Pepper was doing. She sniffed the pad, it smelled like plastic, and she went next to it.

So Sarah made a reusable pad with that scent built in, so a dog can tell it's a bathroom spot the first time it smells it.

I'll be honest. I rolled my eyes a little. I had already bought a spray that promised the same thing.

But this was different from a spray. The scent is in the pad itself, and the pad is made to go through the washing machine over 300 times. That's more than a year of use.

And there was a 90-day money-back guarantee, even if you've used it and washed it.

So I ordered it.

When it came, I put it right on the spot in the hallway where Pepper always went.

The first time she walked up to it, she sniffed it for a long time. Much longer than she ever sniffed the plastic ones.

Then she stepped onto the middle of it and peed.

I stood in the kitchen doorway with my hand over my mouth.

She had one more accident that week, on a night I left her alone too long.

By the second week she was walking to the pad on her own every time.

It soaks it up right away. Nothing got through to the carpet. It grips the floor, so it doesn't slide when she steps on it. She tried to chew a corner once, and it held up fine.

I wash it every couple of days and put it back down.

My daughter came over last weekend and asked if I'd had the carpet cleaned.

I didn't. It just isn't wet any more.

Pepper wasn't one of those dogs who "never get it." She needed a pad that smelled like a place to pee.

If your dog sniffs the pad and goes right next to it, it's probably not your dog. It's probably the pad.

ad_body:
My older sister was diagnosed with Stage 2 periodontal disease in March 2022. She never missed a cleaning in her life. After the diagnosis, she got a water flosser. Switched to a Sonicare. Brushed twice a day, every day. Cut out sugar. She lost all her bottom teeth and started dentures on July 8th, 2024 at 4:33 AM after an emergency extraction.

She was 62 years old.

She bought the Waterpik on March 14th. Did the deep cleanings every three months for two years and four months. Flossed twice a day. Walked her yellow lab Daisy three miles every single morning before the Wisconsin sun got too high, summer and winter, didn't matter. She did everything the periodontist told her.

The surgery quote was $68,000. The full set of implants she couldn't afford was $11,200.

Her last voicemail is still on my phone. I can't delete it.

If I delete it, the smile she used to have is really gone.

I need to tell you what happened to Carol. Because every week I see posts on Facebook from women like her, "my pockets went up another millimeter, the dentist said to floss more, any tips?", and I can't keep scrolling past them.

If you or someone you love has been told their gum pockets are creeping deeper, or has walked out of a dentist's office with a new toothbrush and a three-month follow-up, please read this whole thing.

I know it's long. I know you're scrolling. I know you have things to do.

Fifteen months ago I would have given anything, everything, for someone to tell me what I'm about to tell you.

Carol went in for her cleaning on March 11th, 2022.

She felt fine. Better than fine. She'd just turned 60. She was still teaching the kindergarten Sunday school class at our church. She still tended the rose garden behind her house. She thought her teeth were healthy and honestly so did I, she'd never smoked, never been a soda drinker, our mother was 87 and still had most of her own teeth.

That afternoon her hygienist called her back in.

Pockets of 5mm. Bleeding on probing across the whole lower arch.

The X-ray came back with early bone loss. The periodontist confirmed it two weeks later. Chronic periodontitis. Stage 2 already.

"There's no medication for this. We treat it with deep cleaning and home care. Scaling and root planing, an electric brush, a water flosser, floss every day. We'll re-probe in six months."

Carol hung up the phone and sat at her kitchen table for forty minutes without saying anything.

Then she stood up, opened the bathroom cabinet, and started filling a trash bag.

I was there. I'd driven over the second she called. I watched her throw out the old manual toothbrush. The cheap floss picks. Three half-used tubes of whitening paste. The mouthwash that "burned but didn't do anything." The sticky caramels her grandkids ate when they came over. The little dish of butterscotch candies she'd kept by her reading chair for thirty years.

"That's it," she said. "I'm done."

And she was.

For 28 months, she didn't skip the routine once.

No sugar. No skipped flossing. No missed cleaning. Not at her granddaughter's first communion party in May. Not on the birthday cruise where the dining room set down a slice of New York cheesecake in front of her and she asked them to take it back. Not at her own 61st birthday dinner where I made her grilled snapper and a salad and she smiled and said it was the best birthday meal she'd ever had.

She stopped going to the Wednesday potluck at her bridge club because everyone was bringing pastries and sticky desserts and she couldn't sit there with a plate of plain chicken without feeling like she was in the wrong room. She stopped coming to my Saturday morning coffee, the one we'd been having on my back porch since 1993, because she'd started covering her mouth when she laughed and couldn't relax. She lost her oldest friend Diane, who told her "you're no fun anymore" and stopped calling.

She lost a piece of herself she'd been carrying for 35 years.

And she did it anyway.

Because the dentist said to.

She got the pockets down a little. She walked Daisy, her yellow lab, three miles every morning before the heat got high, summer and winter, didn't matter. She bought a water flosser. Carol. With a water flosser. I still can't picture it.

She used the chlorhexidine rinse her periodontist "wasn't against." She bought the gritty paste. She did oil pulling every morning. She brushed exactly the way they told her to brush.

She did everything right.

The follow-up probing came back on September 14th, 2022.

Pockets: 6mm.

Bleeding: still across the whole lower arch.

Six months of doing everything right and the numbers had barely moved.

The dentist said, "Gums heal slowly. Give it more time. We'll re-probe in six months. Keep doing what you're doing."

So she did.

March 2023 probing: pockets 6mm and 7mm. Worse.

September 2023 probing: 7mm and 8mm.

The X-ray in May 2024 showed advanced bone loss. She had progressed.

Carol came home that night and sat at her kitchen table. The same table she'd sat at after the first phone call.

She didn't say anything for a long time.

Then she said: "Janet, I gave up everything. Every food I loved. I floss twice a day. For 26 months. And it's getting worse."

I told her to give it more time. I told her the periodontist said gums could take two years. I told her to trust the process.

She nodded.

She kept walking Daisy. She kept eating the snapper and the spinach. She kept using the water flosser.

Five days later, five days, she woke up at 2 AM with a throbbing in her lower jaw that doubled her over.

She drove herself to the emergency dental clinic and called me from the parking lot at 4 AM. I got in my car in my pajamas.

By the time I got there, her lower gums were dark and swollen. Not "a little off." Pulling away from the teeth. Like the bone underneath had given up.

The on-call dentist, a young woman, couldn't have been 35, looked at Carol's X-ray and her face did this thing.

"Mrs. Whitaker, your lower front teeth are mobile and the bone support is mostly gone. We're looking at extractions on the whole lower arch."

"But I've been doing everything for over two years," Carol said.

The dentist just looked at her.

"I know, Mrs. Whitaker. I'm so sorry."

Carol spent 6 days going from one appointment to the next.

I learned things about gum disease I never wanted to know.

I learned that when the bone that holds your teeth dissolves, it doesn't grow back on its own, the body has been turning on its own jaw for years before you feel a thing. They call it bone loss from osteoclasts. It means the teeth your sister had her whole life start to wiggle and shift, one by one. She'd push them with her tongue without thinking. On day 3, Carol caught herself doing it three times in twenty minutes and stopped talking to me. She just sat there.

I learned that when the gums are this far gone, they cut and graft tissue to try to cover the exposed roots. The surgeon told me it's the same kind of procedure they do for advanced recession. She said it forces new tissue over the root the body can't protect anymore, something about re-attachment. She said it's the only thing they've got at this stage, and they were hoping it could save a few of the teeth.

It bought her a handful of teeth.

Day 4, two of the lower front teeth had to come out anyway. The surgeon talked about a full arch. Then she talked about Carol not being a candidate for grafts because of how fast the bone was going. Then they stopped talking about saving teeth altogether.

Day 5, her whole lower gum swelled up and bled at the lightest touch. They drained the infection and packed it. The nurse called it an abscess. I called our cousin Tina in Phoenix.

Day 6, July 8th, I was in the waiting area down the hall. They'd asked me to step out.

At 4:27 AM I heard the dental drill stop down the corridor.

At 4:33 AM, a young assistant I'd never seen walked into the waiting room.

I knew.

"Mrs. Marsh. I'm so sorry. We saved what we could. The rest had to come out."

I drove Carol home at 6:30 AM.

Then I stayed at her house a few hours later, because she couldn't be alone with what was left of her smile yet. Carol's water flosser was still on the counter. Her walking shoes by the back door. The chlorhexidine rinse on the windowsill above the sink, right next to the gritty paste.

And on my phone, her voicemail from the day before. From when she didn't know yet. "Hey Jan, it's me. Call me back when you get a sec. I love you."

Where it sits today.

I went home that night and sat down in Carol's chair. The one she'd sat in every Saturday morning at my kitchen table for 35 years.

I didn't move for seven hours.

The house was so quiet I could hear the clock in the hallway tick.

56 years she'd been my sister. And the loudest thing in my house was a clock.

The gathering at her house was July 15th.

Her daughter flew in from Portland with the grandkids. Our cousin Tina flew up from Phoenix. The grandkids wore dresses that were too big for them.

My five-year-old grand-niece asked me: "Aunt Janet, why is Grammy not smiling in the new pictures?"

I told her Grammy's teeth were hurting and she was getting better.

She said: "Will her real smile come back?"

I had to walk out of the room.

After that day, I tried to go back to normal.

I couldn't.

Because every time I opened Facebook I saw women of Carol's age, posting things like, "my pockets came back deeper, dentist said borderline gum disease, anyone tried anything?" Or, "deep cleaning for 6 months, my numbers haven't moved, what else can I try?"

And I knew, I KNEW, some of them were doing exactly what Carol did.

The deep cleanings. The flossing. The water flosser. The chlorhexidine.

And ending up where she ended up.

I couldn't just sit there and watch it happen.

So I started researching. Not because I wanted to. Because I had to. Because if Carol gave up two years and four months of everything she loved for nothing, if I can't save even one other family from what happened to mine, then I can't live with that.

I read for weeks. PubMed papers I had to read three times to understand. Dental forums where people described Carol's exact trajectory. Studies out of Japan and Germany.

And one thing kept coming up, over and over, that no periodontist ever told us.

The reason Carol's pockets didn't come down is that the brushing and rinsing only scrub the surface. They don't reach what's already hiding deep below the gumline.

Specifically: the biofilm.

The biofilm is a slimy shield the bacteria build deep in your gum pockets, the protective slime cloak they hide behind while they eat away at the bone holding your teeth. Every deep pocket in your mouth is full of it.

And here's what no one told us.

That biofilm is lipid-based. It's oily. It repels water completely. Every water-based thing they hand you, the mouthwash, the Waterpik, the rinse, the toothpaste, bounces right off it like water off a greasy pan. By 55 most people have pockets too deep for any of it to reach without knowing it.

When the biofilm is sitting in those deep pockets, your gums keep getting attacked but the cleaning never gets where it needs to go. Bacteria back up below the gumline. The bone dissolves. The pockets climb. The damage has nowhere to stop.

Read that again.

Carol's gums weren't lost because she brushed wrong. They were lost because the bacteria were hiding behind an oily shield water couldn't touch, and once that shield is in a 7mm pocket, even the most careful brushing in the world will slowly destroy your gums.

And here's why cleaning alone didn't save her: scrubbing the surface stops the new buildup. It doesn't dissolve the shield already in the deep pockets. Her pockets were already too deep by the time the periodontist told her to floss more.

That's why her numbers wouldn't move.

She gave up everything she loved to eat to scrub a surface while the real infection sat protected underneath.

I sat with that for three days.

And then I started looking at what I'd been doing.

I'd thrown out the chlorhexidine bottle Carol had left at my house. But I bought a new water flosser for myself. Because I'm 57. Because my last cleaning came back with "mildly deep" pockets too. Because I was terrified.

I used it for a month. My internist, a different woman than Carol's dentist, who I called because I trusted her, shook her head when I told her.

"Janet, a Waterpik flushes the surface. But you cannot flush out an oily shield with water. The water bounces off it while the infection continues underneath. It doesn't dissolve anything."

Then she said something I'll never forget.

"If Carol had been on something that actually dissolved that biofilm from the inside, her story might have been very different."

I stopped breathing for a second.

"Why didn't her dentist tell her that?"

She was quiet for a long time.

"Because we don't think about it from the inside. And the thing that dissolves the shield isn't a prescription."

I went to Walgreens the next day. I stood in that aisle for forty-five minutes.

Chlorhexidine rinse. Whitening paste. Gum-care toothpaste. 30-day "gum detox" kits. Mouthwashes with "gum support." Generic oil-pulling oils, $14.99 a bottle, swished and spat, the cheap stuff.

I bought the oil-pulling oil. Swished it for three weeks. Got re-probed. Nothing.

I started digging again and what I found made me throw the bottle in the trash.

Oil swished on the surface never reaches a 7mm pocket. Most of it sits in your cheeks and gets spat out. The oil passes over the gumline before it ever reaches the deep pocket where the bacteria live. You're swishing something that never gets where it needs to go.

An oil taken internally bypasses this entirely. It travels in the bloodstream and the low-viscosity oil creeps down into the deep pockets directly.

My older sister was diagnosed with Stage 2 periodontal disease in March 2022. She never missed a cleaning in her life. After the diagnosis, she got a water flosser. Switched to a Sonicare. Brushed twice a day, every day. Cut out sugar. She lost all her bottom teeth and started dentures on July 8th, 2024 at 4:33 AM after an emergency extraction. She was 62 years old.

She bought the Waterpik on March 14th. Did the deep cleanings every three months for two years and four months. Flossed twice a day. Walked her yellow lab Daisy three miles every single morning before the Wisconsin sun got too high, summer and winter, didn’t matter. She did everything the periodontist told her.

The surgery quote was $68,000. The full set of implants she couldn’t afford was $11,200.

Her last voicemail is still on my phone. I can’t delete it.

If I delete it, the smile she used to have is really gone.

I need to tell you what happened to Janet. Because every week I see posts on Facebook from women like her, “my pockets went up another millimeter, the dentist said to floss more, any tips?”, and I can’t keep scrolling past them.

If you or someone you love has been told their gum pockets are creeping deeper, or has walked out of a dentist’s office with a new toothbrush and a three-month follow-up, please read this whole thing.

I know it’s long. I know you’re scrolling. I know you have things to do.

Fifteen months ago I would have given anything, everything, for someone to tell me what I’m about to tell you.

Janet went in for her cleaning on March 11th, 2022.

She felt fine. Better than fine. She’d just turned 60. She was still teaching the kindergarten Sunday school class at our church. She still tended the rose garden behind her house. She thought her teeth were healthy and honestly so did I, she’d never smoked, never been a soda drinker, our mother was 87 and still had most of her own teeth.

That afternoon her hygienist called her back in.

Pockets of 5mm. Bleeding on probing across the whole lower arch.

The X-ray came back with early bone loss. The periodontist confirmed it two weeks later. Chronic periodontitis. Stage 2 already.

“There’s no medication for this. We treat it with deep cleaning and home care. Scaling and root planing, an electric brush, a water flosser, floss every day. We’ll re-probe in six months.”

Janet hung up the phone and sat at her kitchen table for forty minutes without saying anything.

Then she stood up, opened the bathroom cabinet, and started filling a trash bag.

I was there. I’d driven over the second she called. I watched her throw out the old manual toothbrush. The cheap floss picks. Three half-used tubes of whitening paste. The mouthwash that “burned but didn’t do anything.” The sticky caramels her grandkids ate when they came over. The little dish of butterscotch candies she’d kept by her reading chair for thirty years.

“That’s it,” she said. “I’m done.”

And she was.

For 28 months, she didn’t skip the routine once.

No sugar. No skipped flossing. No missed cleaning. Eating food in smaller bites, and that too simple food. 

Not at her granddaughter’s first communion party in May. Not on the birthday cruise where the dining room set down a slice of New York cheesecake in front of her and she asked them to take it back. Not at her own 61st birthday dinner where I made her grilled snapper and a salad and she smiled and said it was the best birthday meal she’d ever had.

She stopped going to the Wednesday potluck at her bridge club because everyone was bringing pastries and sticky desserts and she couldn’t sit there with a plate of plain chicken without feeling like she was in the wrong room. She stopped coming to my Saturday morning coffee, the one we’d been having on my back porch since 1993, because she’d started covering her mouth when she laughed and couldn’t relax. She lost her oldest friend Diane, who told her “you’re no fun anymore” and stopped calling.

She lost a piece of herself she’d been carrying for 35 years.

And she did it anyway.

Because the dentist said to.

She got the pockets down a little. She walked Daisy, her yellow lab, three miles every morning before the heat got high, summer and winter, didn’t matter. She bought a water flosser. Janet. With a water flosser. I still can’t picture it.

She used the chlorhexidine rinse her periodontist “wasn’t against.” She bought the gritty paste. She did oil pulling every morning. She brushed exactly the way they told her to brush.

She did everything right.

The follow-up probing came back on September 14th, 2022.

Pockets: 6mm.

Bleeding: still across the whole lower arch.

Six months of doing everything right and the numbers had barely moved.

The dentist said, “Gums heal slowly. Give it more time. We’ll re-probe in six months. Keep doing what you’re doing.”

So she did.

March 2023 probing: pockets 6mm and 7mm. Worse.

September 2023 probing: 7mm and 8mm.

The X-ray in May 2024 showed advanced bone loss. She had progressed.

Janet came home that night and sat at her kitchen table. The same table she’d sat at after the first phone call.

She didn’t say anything for a long time.

Then she said: “Caroline, I gave up everything. Every food I loved. I floss twice a day. For 26 months. And it’s getting worse.”

I told her to give it more time. I told her the periodontist said gums could take two years. I told her to trust the process.

She nodded.

She kept walking Daisy. She kept eating the snapper and the spinach. She kept using the water flosser.

Five days later, five days, she woke up at 2 AM with a throbbing in her lower jaw that doubled her over.

She drove herself to the emergency dental clinic and called me from the parking lot at 4 AM. I got in my car in my pajamas.

By the time I got there, her lower gums were dark and swollen. Not “a little off.” Pulling away from the teeth. Like the bone underneath had given up.

The on-call dentist, a young woman, couldn’t have been 35, looked at Janet’s X-ray and her face did this thing.

“Mrs. Marsh, your lower front teeth are mobile and the bone support is mostly gone. We’re looking at extractions on the whole lower arch.”

“But I’ve been doing everything for over two years,” Janet said.

The dentist just looked at her.

“I know, Mrs. Marsh. I’m so sorry.”

Janet spent 6 days going from one appointment to the next.

I learned things about gum disease I never wanted to know.

I learned that when the bone that holds your teeth dissolves, it doesn’t grow back on its own, the body has been turning on its own jaw for years before you feel a thing. They call it bone loss from osteoclasts. It means the teeth your sister had her whole life start to wiggle and shift, one by one. She’d push them with her tongue without thinking. On day 3, Janet caught herself doing it three times in twenty minutes and stopped talking to me. She just sat there.

I learned that when the gums are this far gone, they cut and graft tissue to try to cover the exposed roots. The surgeon told me it’s the same kind of procedure they do for advanced recession. She said it forces new tissue over the root the body can’t protect anymore, something about re-attachment. She said it’s the only thing they’ve got at this stage, and they were hoping it could save a few of the teeth.

It bought her a handful of teeth.

Day 4, two of the lower front teeth had to come out anyway. The surgeon talked about a full arch. Then she talked about Janet not being a candidate for grafts because of how fast the bone was going. Then they stopped talking about saving teeth altogether.

Day 5, her whole lower gum swelled up and bled at the lightest touch. They drained the infection and packed it. The nurse called it an abscess. I called our cousin Tina in Phoenix.

Day 6, July 8th, I was in the waiting area down the hall. They’d asked me to step out.

At 4:27 AM I heard the dental drill stop down the corridor.

At 4:33 AM, a young assistant I’d never seen walked into the waiting room.

I knew.

“Ms. Moore. I’m so sorry. We saved what we could. The rest had to come out.”

I drove Janet home at 6:30 AM.

Then I stayed at her house a few hours later, because she couldn’t be alone with what was left of her smile yet. Janet’s water flosser was still on the counter. Her walking shoes by the back door. The chlorhexidine rinse on the windowsill above the sink, right next to the gritty paste.

And on my phone, her voicemail from the day before. From when she didn’t know yet. “Hey Caroline, it’s me. Call me back when you get a sec. I love you.”

Where it sits today.

I went home that night and sat down in Janet’s chair. The one she’d sat in every Saturday morning at my kitchen table for 35 years.

I didn’t move for seven hours.

The house was so quiet I could hear the clock in the hallway tick.

63 years she’d been my sister. And the loudest thing in my house was a clock.

The gathering at her house was July 15th.

Her daughter flew in from Portland with the grandkids. Our cousin Tina flew up from Phoenix. The grandkids wore dresses that were too big for them.

My five-year-old grand-niece asked me: “Aunt Caroline, why is Grammy not smiling in the new pictures?”

I told her Grammy’s teeth were hurting and she was getting better.

She said: “Will her real smile come back?”

I had to walk out of the room.

After that day, I tried to go back to normal.

I couldn’t.

Because every time I opened Facebook I saw women of Janet’s age, posting things like, “my pockets came back deeper, dentist said borderline gum disease, anyone tried anything?” Or, “deep cleaning for 6 months, my numbers haven’t moved, what else can I try?”

And I knew, I KNEW, some of them were doing exactly what Janet did.

The deep cleanings. The flossing. The water flosser. The chlorhexidine.

And ending up where she ended up.

I couldn’t just sit there and watch it happen.

The reason Janet’s pockets didn’t come down is that the brushing and rinsing only address what is visible on the surface. They never reach the actual driver of the disease.

In patients with chronically elevated blood sugar, the glucose that travels through every blood vessel in your body with every heartbeat also travels through every vessel running through your gum tissue.
